questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: For what someone is doing at this moment, English uses the -ing form and so does Hindi. जाता है is the habit, not the moment, and mapping it onto English 'is going' is the single commonest error in this module.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The auxiliary tracks the person, and मैं always takes हूँ. This is the same होना table from Module 5, unchanged.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Changing the participle to feminine does not change the auxiliary. मैं takes हूँ regardless of the speaker's gender.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: तुम is grammatically plural, so the participle is खाते. The singular participle never appears with हो.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: For one completed trip you need the perfective. वह जाता था describes a routine he kept, which is a different claim entirely.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: होगा looks like a future because it contains हो, but the presumptive is a guess about a habit. The real future arrives in level twenty-two.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: हूँ belongs to मैं. The auxiliary is chosen by the person of the subject, never by the verb.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Not ungrammatical, but it means he rather than she. The mistake changes the meaning rather than merely sounding wrong.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: हो belongs to तुम. Mixing आप with a तुम auxiliary sounds like starting a sentence politely and finishing it casually.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: थे is the masculine plural. Getting the participle feminine and then leaving the auxiliary masculine is the usual half-correction here.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: थे is the masculine plural. One speaker is singular, so था — the auxiliary is counting, not identifying who is talking.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: आप never takes singular agreement, however few people you are addressing.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The continuous is built on the bare stem, never on the habitual participle. The two bases do not stack.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: करता is the habitual participle. The continuous needs the bare stem कर, with nothing added to it at all.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: A word meaning right now cannot sit with the habitual. If the sentence points at this moment, the aspect has to be continuous.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The auxiliary carries gender in the past. Making the participle feminine and leaving था masculine is the usual half-correction.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: थीं is feminine plural, and it would need the participle खाती in front of it. The two halves must agree with each other.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Not ungrammatical, but it means he rather than she. वह is genderless, so the marker is the only thing telling your listener who you mean.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: बोलते is the habitual participle. Only the bare stem can carry the continuous marker.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Deleting what looks like a repeated word removes the verb and leaves only the marker. Both are needed.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: There is only ever one auxiliary. The past replaces the present one rather than being added behind it.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: तुम is grammatically plural whatever the past tense is doing, so both agreeing words stay plural.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: रोज़ describes a repeated habit, and the continuous can only describe one stretch of time in progress.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: आता है is the habitual — he comes, as a routine. The perfective is about one completed arrival.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Not ungrammatical, but it means he. वह tells your listener nothing about gender, so the participle is doing all of that work.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The marker and the auxiliary always match in this cell. Mixing them is audible even before you analyse it.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The marker agrees with हम, not with anything the sentence is about. Mixing रही with थे breaks the rhyme.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
options: मैं सो रहा था और फिर मैं सो रहा था
questions.explanation_en: Splitting the stem from its marker breaks the verb apart. नहीं goes in front of the group, never inside it.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: बैठ रहा है means he is in the act of lowering himself into a chair. For someone already seated, Hindi uses the perfective.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The participle goes plural along with the auxiliary. Fixing only one of the two is the recurring half-correction in this module.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The nasalised गईं is a real form, but it does not appear in front of an auxiliary. हैं is already carrying the plural.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Naming a plain past time calls for the bare perfective. था would imply that something else happened after it and you are measuring back from that.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: थे is plural. One speaker is singular whatever their person, so the auxiliary is था.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: बैठ रहा था describes the movement into the chair. For someone already seated, Hindi uses the perfective.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
options: मैं सो रहा था और फिर मैं सो रहा था
questions.explanation_en: होगा is a guess about a habit, not a plan for tomorrow. The real future is a different form entirely.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: है ties the result to the present, which clashes with कल pointing at yesterday. Naming a past time forces the bare form.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
options: मैं सो रहा था और फिर मैं सो रहा था
questions.explanation_en: The participle and the auxiliary both carry gender here, so they cannot disagree with each other.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The plural is marked once, not twice. With थीं present, the participle does not nasalise.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: तुम takes plural agreement on both words in every tense, however many people you are addressing.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: होगा is singular. The presumptive counts and genders exactly as the past auxiliary does.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: होगा is singular. The presumptive counts in the third person exactly as the past auxiliary does.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: There is no auxiliary in the future. Adding one is the natural reflex after twenty levels of participle plus होना, and it is wrong.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Getting the gender right does not fix the person. -एगी belongs to वह, and the middle of the word is what identifies मैं.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: The stem vowel and the ending vowel merge into one long ऊँ. Writing both out separately is a spelling error rather than a grammatical one, but it is a visible one.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: नहीं comes before the verb, not after it. Putting it at the end sounds like an afterthought rather than a refusal.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: होगा belongs to the third person. मैं has its own form, built from the हूँ you have used since Module 5.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: -ऊँगा belongs to मैं. In the future the ending identifies the person, so the wrong ending names the wrong person.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Not ungrammatical, but it means he. With no auxiliary present, this single letter is doing all the work.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: खाता is the habitual participle of the verb. The object here is the noun खाना, which happens to look identical to the infinitive.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: -ओगे belongs to तुम. Opening politely with आप and finishing casually is more noticeable than a plain grammatical slip.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: An imperative takes no auxiliary and usually no pronoun either. The form alone is the whole sentence.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: आओ is the तुम form. Opening with आप and finishing with a casual imperative is the mismatch most likely to land badly.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: Not a grammatical error — a social one. With anyone you have just met, the bare stem is the wrong choice however correct it looks.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: होया is what the rule predicts and it is not a word. होना and जाना are the two verbs where the perfective is built from a changed stem.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
options: मैं सो रहा था और फिर मैं सो रहा था
questions.explanation_en: चलाया is a different verb — चलाना, meaning to drive or operate something. Adding a syllable changes the word rather than the tense.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: बोलते is the habitual participle and needs an auxiliary behind it. The imperative is built from the bare stem instead.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: करिए is what the rule predicts and it is not what people say. This is one of exactly four verbs where that happens.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: नहीं negates statements. An instruction takes मत, and using the wrong one is immediately audible.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: बात is one of the feminine nouns Module 4 asked you to memorise, and the perfective agrees with it like any other participle.

questions.prompt_en: Which of these is the grammatically correct sentence/phrase?
questions.explanation_en: A transitive verb in the perfective needs ने on the subject. That construction arrives in Module 9, which is why these four are recognition only for now.
